metadata.dataset_description: This dataset comprises 500 simulated entries from the ServiceNow `fm_expense_line` table, which tracks various attributes of financial expenses. Key fields include 'number', 'opened_at', 'amount', 'state', 'short_description', 'ci', 'user', 'department', 'category', 'process_date', 'source_id', and 'type'. The table provides a comprehensive record of financial transactions, capturing the expense amount, departmental allocation, and the nature of each expense. It offers a detailed view of organizational expenditures across various categories, highlighting both the timing and the approval status of each financial entry.
metadata.goal: Examine how the cost of an expense impacts its processing time, with the goal of improving the efficiency and equity of expense report processing across all cost levels.

predicted_insights: Lower-cost claims (~$1k) take over 5 times longer on average than higher-cost claims (~$11.7k), suggesting small expenses face disproportionate delays that could be targeted to improve processing equity and efficiency.

This 5.6 percentage-point gap represents 7 extra Pending/Submitted cases per 125 items in the lowest quartile; eliminating this disparity would reduce open low-amount items by ~11% (7/65), helping small expenses clear more equitably.

The relationship between expense amount and processing speed is generally weak (range ≈ -0.187 to 0.067), and notably negative in HR and IT, implying that higher-cost reports may be processed slightly faster there—an equity signal worth auditing to ensure consistent handling across cost levels.

Within the highest-cost quartile, declines (26.4%) nearly match processed outcomes (27.2%), and 46.4% are still pending or just submitted, indicating high-cost expenses face heavier scrutiny and slower completion.

Across all 7 departments, the relationship between expense amount and processing time is very weak (all |ρ| < 0.19), with HR (-0.187) and IT (-0.154) showing the strongest negative associations, suggesting higher-cost reports there may be processed slightly faster.

At least half of expenses in every cost quartile are processed the same day (0 days), indicating no median-level delay for higher-cost reports; the inefficiency comes from a smaller tail of cases (max 28 days) rather than systemic cost-related slowness, so focusing interventions on outliers could improve equity and efficiency.

Highest-cost expenses have the lowest delay rate (19.2%) while mid-range Q2 is highest (28.0%), an 8.8 percentage-point gap that suggests high-value reports may be prioritized and that streamlining mid-tier processing could improve equity.

Across all departments, higher-cost expenses are processed faster than lower-cost ones (Q4–Q1 differences are all negative), with disparities ranging from about -1.19 (Customer Support) to -4.18 (Sales), suggesting potential equity issues for lower-cost submissions.

Across the observed range (≈94 to ≈14,786 units), higher-cost expenses are predicted to be processed about 4.19 days faster than lower-cost ones, and a 1 SD increase in amount (~3,300 units) corresponds to ~0.94 fewer processing days—indicating larger expenses tend to move quicker, which may raise equity concerns.

Across 20 amount bins spanning about 419 to 12,898 units, the mean predicted Decline probability remains constant at 0.50, indicating decisions are amount-agnostic and suggesting any inequities by cost level are unlikely to come from higher rejection rates.

End-of-month high-amount submissions take 30% longer to process (3.5 vs 2.6923 days), suggesting a bottleneck near month-end; prioritizing or smoothing workload then could improve equity and efficiency across cost levels.

All regions exhibit negative slopes (from -0.72 to -1.66 days per $1,000), meaning higher-cost expenses are processed faster, with South America having the strongest acceleration (-1.6636 days per $1,000) and Europe the weakest (-0.7182), suggesting potential prioritization of larger expenses that varies by location.
predicted_summary:
Higher-cost expenses move faster through processing. Among Processed expenses, average processing_time drops from about 15.4 days near $1.0k to about 3.0 days near $11.7k (Pearson r = -0.72; slope ≈ -0.00107 days per dollar; R² = 0.51). This pattern holds even after accounting for department, location, state, and user: each additional 1,000 units of amount is associated with roughly 0.285 fewer days (≈6.8 hours) of processing_time (β = -0.000285; R² = 0.631; n = 500).
Delays cluster more in lower-cost expenses. While the median processing_time is 0.0 days in every amount quartile (indicating many same-day completions), the share of expenses taking more than 1 day is higher in lower quartiles (Q1 24.8%; Q2 28.0%; Q3 24.8%) than in the highest quartile (Q4 19.2%). Lower-cost expenses are also more likely to sit in non-Processed states: 52% in Q1 vs 46.4% in Q4.
The amount–time relationship varies across departments, locations, and submission timing. Customer Support shows the largest low–high amount gap in average processing_time (Q4–Q1 ≈ -1.19 days, i.e., faster for higher amounts), while Development is an outlier with a slight positive amount–time correlation (Spearman ≈ +0.0666 vs negatives elsewhere, e.g., HR -0.1870, IT -0.1535). By location, Europe exhibits the steepest decrease in processing_time as amount rises (≈ -0.7182 days per $1,000 among Processed expenses). For high-amount expenses (≥ 7,992.29), submitting in the last 7 days of a month is linked to longer processing_time (3.5 vs 2.6923 days), and despite speed differences, the likelihood of Decline does not change with amount once department, location, and user are controlled (odds ratio ≈ 1.00).
